rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari links God's unrestricted provision to His power over the cosmic alternation of night and day and life and death, concluding that He can transfer rule from Persians to Arabs.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ذكر قدرته الباهرة، فذكر حال الليل والنهار في المعاقبة بينهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan endorses al-Zamakhshari's explanation that the same power can transfer dominion and honor between peoples.
rows.anchor: ويؤتيه العرب ويعزهم. انتهى. وهو حسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question in “Have you not seen” expresses astonishment.
rows.anchor: الاستفهام الذي معناه التعجب في ألم تر إلى الذين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The partitive “some of the Scripture” implies that they did not master or preserve the Torah, disparaging their claimed righteousness.
rows.anchor: فإدخال: من، يدل على أنهم لم يحيطوا بالتوراة علما ولا حفظا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “that is because” points to their turning away, caused by their fabrication.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله ذلك بأنهم إشارة إلى توليهم وإعراضهم اللذين سببهما افتراؤهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that every soul is paid in full signifies that none of the recompense for its deeds is reduced.
rows.anchor: وفي ووفيت كل نفس إشارة إلى أن جزاء أعمالهم لا ينقص منه شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repetition of “a portion of the Scripture” and “summoned to God's Book” is either semantic and verbal repetition if they mean the same thing, or verbal repetition alone if they differ.
rows.anchor: والتكرار في نصيبا من الكتاب يدعون إلى كتاب الله إما في اللفظ والمعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pairing of turning away and withdrawal is another repetition, semantic if synonymous and otherwise only verbal.
rows.anchor: وفي التولي والإعراض إن كانا بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated forms of “Master of dominion,” giving and removing dominion magnify the idea if synonymous, or repeat only the wording if distinct.
rows.anchor: وفي: مالك الملك تؤتي الملك وتنزع الملك وتكراره في جمل للتفخيم والتعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated “whom You will” and the repeated clauses about merging and bringing forth likewise serve as verbal or semantic repetition.
rows.anchor: وتكرار من تشاء وفي تولج وفي تخرج وفي متعلقيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpreters take the preposition “in” in the night-day clauses to mean “over”; the imagery of insertion then conveys dominance and covering.
rows.anchor: على قول من زعم ذلك في قوله تولج الليل في النهار أي على النهار

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj reads the negation in “There is no doubt in it” as an implied command: do not doubt it.
rows.anchor: على قول الزجاج، أي لا ترتابوا فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording “Master of dominion” is an example of matching wordplay.
rows.anchor: والتجنيس المماثل في مالك الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage uses antithesis in giving versus removing, honoring versus humbling, and night versus day and living versus dead.
rows.anchor: والطباق: في: تؤتي وتنزع، وتعز وتذل، وفي الليل والنهار، وفي الحي والميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated wording beginning with “You merge” returns the end of the clause to its beginning.
rows.anchor: ورد العجز على الصدر في: تولج، وما بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ellipsis supplies the omitted complement in “You give dominion to whom You will”: whom You will to give it to.
rows.anchor: كقوله تؤتي الملك من تشاء أي من تشاء أن تؤتيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book is figuratively made the agent of judgment because it clarifies the rulings and thereby causes judgment.
rows.anchor: والإسناد المجازي في ليحكم بينهم أسند الحكم إلى الكتاب لأنه يبين الأحكام فهو سبب الحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects the appeal to the Prophet's statement “Whoever cheats is not one of us” because the cited al-Nabigha line differs from the verse.
rows.anchor: بقوله عليه السلام: «من غشنا فليس منا» ليس بجيد لما بيناه من الفرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception branches from the purpose clause: believers must not take disbelievers as allies except to avert danger, when outward words or acts may show allegiance while the heart remains unaffectionate.
rows.anchor: تقاة هذا استثناء مفرع من المفعول له

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas calls the permitted dissimulation outward accommodation: a believer among disbelievers may guard the tongue while keeping affection out of the heart.
rows.anchor: ولذلك قال ابن عباس: التقية المشار إليها مداراة ظاهرة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada allows believers surrounded by dominant disbelievers to make agreements and conciliate them to repel harm while remaining inwardly firm in faith.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: إذا كان الكفار غالبين، أو يكون المؤمنون في قوم كفار

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud advises mixing with people, keeping religious distance, and treating them as they prefer without compromising one's religion.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود: خالطوا الناس وزايلوهم وعاملوهم بما يشتهون، ودينكم فلا تثلموه

rows.speaker: صعصعة بن صوحان
rows.claim: Sa'sa'a told Usama ibn Zayd to be close to believers and courteous to disbelievers, since good manners satisfy a disbeliever.
rows.anchor: وقال صعصعة بن صوحان لأسامة بن زيد: خالص المؤمن وخالق الكافر

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: Al-Sadiq says dissimulation is obligatory, illustrating it by hiding behind a mosque pillar from a man who curses him.
rows.anchor: وقال الصادق: التقية واجبة، إني لأسمع الرجل في المسجد يشتمني فأستتر منه بالسارية

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: Al-Sadiq says ostentation toward a believer is associationism, while ostentation toward a hypocrite counts as worship.
rows.anchor: وقال الصادق: التقية واجبة، إني لأسمع الرجل في المسجد يشتمني فأستتر منه بالسارية لئلا يراني. وقال: الرياء مع المؤمن شرك، ومع المنافق عبادة

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل ومجاهد
rows.claim: Muadh ibn Jabal and Mujahid restrict dissimulation to early Islam, before the faith and Muslim strength were established; they say Muslims are now secure from needing it against enemies.
rows.anchor: وقال معاذ بن جبل، ومجاهد: كانت التقية في جدة الإسلام قبل استحكام الدين وقوة المسلمين

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan allows dissimulation until the Day of Resurrection but excludes murder.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: التقية جائزة إلى يوم القيامة، ولا تقية في القتل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets the exception as fear of severing kinship, permitting worldly social contact with disbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: إلا أن تتقوا قطيعة الرحم فخالطوهم في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from third person to direct address in “unless you fear” is eloquent: prohibition avoids confronting believers directly, while the later permission directly addresses them as divine kindness and honor.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله إلا أن تتقوا التفات، لأنه خرج من الغيبة إلى الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read taqāt; Abu Hayyan derives it from waqiya by changing initial wāw to tāʾ and the moving yāʾ to alif, describing a rare verbal-noun pattern rather than the expected ittiqāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: تقاة، وأصله: وقية، فأبدلت الواو تاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line containing iḥtifār is cited as evidence for the unusual verbal-noun form; the poet is unnamed in this passage.
rows.anchor: ولاح بجانب الجبلين منه ... ركام يحفر الأرض احتفارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception means “unless you fear them with fear.”
rows.anchor: والمعنى: إلا أن تخافوا منهم خوفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i uses imāla for taqāt and ḥaqq tuqātihi; Hamza agrees here, Warsh uses an intermediate sound here, and the other readers use fatḥ.
rows.anchor: وأمال الكسائي: تقاة، وحق تقاته، ووافقه حمزة هنا وقرأ ورش بين اللفظين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari glosses the exception as fearing a danger from them that one must guard against.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: إلا أن تخافوا من جهتهم أمرا يجب اتقاؤه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan explains taqāt as a passive-noun form used as an object, not as a verbal noun, which is why al-Zamakhshari paraphrases it as fearing something.
rows.anchor: فجعل: تقاة، مصدرا في موضع اسم المفعول، فانتصابه على أنه مفعول به

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali allows taqāt to be a circumstantial plural of fāʿil, though that singular is unattested, or a plural of taqī.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي: يجوز أن يكون: تقاة، مثل: رماة، حالا من: تتقوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects the plural analysis as very weak: taqī would normally pluralize as atqiyāʾ, and the analogy kamī/kamāh is irregular; ḥaqq tuqātihi confirms the verbal-noun meaning “right fear of Him.”
rows.anchor: وتجويز كونه جمعا ضعيف جدا، ولو كان جمع: تقي، لكان أتقياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source compares the nouns taqāt and taqiyya through the expression about the prince's blow to the person struck.
rows.anchor: للمتقي تقاة وتقية، كقولهم: ضرب الأمير لمضروبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Raja, Qatada, al-Dahhak, Abu Haywa, Yaqub, Sahl, Hamid ibn Qays, and al-Mufaddal from Asim read taqiyya, a rare faʿīla verbal noun, itself unusual as an iftiʿāl derivative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس، ومجاهد، وأبو رجاء، وقتادة، والضحاك، وأبو حيوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's apparent meaning permits alliance with disbelievers when they are feared.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الآية يقتضي جواز موالاتهم عند الخوف منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes agree that heartfelt alliance with disbelievers is forbidden, as is verbal or behavioral alliance without a necessity of dissimulation; Qur'an and Sunna support this.
rows.anchor: أما الموالاة بالقلب فلا خلاف بين المسلمين في تحريمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person to fear may be any powerful oppressor, including disbelievers, unjust rulers, robbers, influential urban elites, and, according to Malik, a coercive husband.
rows.anchor: فكل قادر غالب يكره بجور منه، فيدخل في ذلك: الكفار، وجورة الرؤساء

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik includes a woman's husband among those who may coerce her and thus be feared.
rows.anchor: قال مالك: وزوج المرأة قد يكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan lists killing, fear for bodily limbs, whipping, threats, and hostility from unjust elites as circumstances that permit dissimulation.
rows.anchor: وأما ما يببحها: فالقتل، والخوف على الجوارح، والضرب بالسوط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Permitted speech can extend from uttering disbelief down to lesser matters such as sale or gift; in actions, any otherwise forbidden act may be allowed.
rows.anchor: فبالكفر فما دونه من: بيع، وهبة، وغير ذلك. وأما من الأفعال: فكل محرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making “the Day” accusative with “He warns you” is weak because of the long separation; attaching it to “the outcome” is also weak because the verbal noun is separated from its complement.
rows.anchor: ويحذركم، لطول الفصل. هذا من جهة اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making “the Day” governed by “powerful over all things” is weak because God's power is constant, not restricted to one day; supplying an omitted verb is also disfavored as ellipsis.
rows.anchor: ويضعف نصبه: بقدير، لأن قدرته على كل شيء لا تختص بيوم دون يوم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari makes “the Day” accusative with “you wish” and takes the pronoun “between it” to refer to Judgment Day, when each soul finds its good and evil present and longs for great distance.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: يوم تجد منصوب: بتود، والضمير في: بينه، ليوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though initially attractive, al-Zamakhshari's parse raises a disputed grammar issue: whether a verb's subject pronoun may refer back to an antecedent attached to that verb's complement.
rows.anchor: والظاهر في بادىء النظر حسنه وترجيحه، إذ يظهر أنه ليس فيه شيء من مضعفات الأقوال السابقة

rows.speaker: الكسائي وهشام وجمهور البصريين
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i, Hisham, and most Basrans permit a subject pronoun to refer to something attached to the verb's complement, which licenses al-Zamakhshari's construction.
rows.anchor: فذهب الكسائي، وهشام، وجمهور البصريين: إلى جواز هذه المسائل

rows.speaker: الفراء وأبو الحسن الأخفش وغيرهما
rows.claim: Al-Farra, Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash, and other Basrans disallow such constructions because the optional complement would become obligatory merely to provide an antecedent for the subject pronoun.
rows.anchor: وذهب الفراء، وأبو الحسن الأخفش، وغيره من البصريين إلى أن هذه المسائل وأمثالها لا تجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan favors the permissive grammatical analysis and cites a line of poetry to support it.
rows.anchor: والصحيح جواز ذلك قال الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “find” most naturally takes one object, “what she did,” with “present” as a circumstantial phrase; alternatively it means “know” and takes two objects, making “present” the second.
rows.anchor: و: تجد، الظاهر أنها متعدية إلى واحد وهو: ما عملت، فيكون بمعنى نصيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What she did” may be a relative clause with its pronoun omitted, or a verbal noun intended as the passive object, with an implied “recompense” or “reward.”
rows.anchor: وما، في: ما عملت، موصولة، والعائد عليها من الصلة محذوف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reported interpretation takes “present” to mean complete and undiminished.
rows.anchor: قيل: ومعنى: محضرا على هذا موفرا غير مبخوس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says the deeds are seen written in scrolls brought before the person as glad tidings, so reward follows after the work is seen.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ترى ما عملت مكتوبا في الصحف محضرا إليها تبشيرا لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read muḥḍaran with fatḥa on ḍād as a passive participle; Ubayy ibn Umayr reads muḥḍiran with kasra, suggesting something hastened or carried quickly to Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: محضرا، بفتح الضاد، اسم مفعول. وقرأ عبيد بن عمير: محضرا بكسر الضاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What she did of evil” can coordinate with what she did of good, functioning as a second object or as an understood circumstantial phrase; “you wish” may then be independent or circumstantial.
rows.anchor: و: ما عملت من سوء، يجوز أن تكون في موضع نصب، معطوفا على: ما عملت من خير

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes “you wish” as a circumstantial clause and refers “between it” to the Day.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون: تود، في موضع الحال أي: وادة تباعد ما بينها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects referring the pronoun to the Day as far-fetched, since the soul would then wish distance from a day that also contains its good; the nearest and better referent is its evil deed.
rows.anchor: وأبعد الزمخشري في عوده على اليوم، لأن أحد القسمين اللذين أحضر له في ذلك اليوم هو: الخير

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari supports coordinating the evil deed with the good deed and treating “you wish” as a circumstantial clause.
rows.anchor: وإلى عطف: ما عملت من سوء، على: ما عملت من خير، وكون، تود، في موضع الحال ذهب إليه الطبري

rows.speaker: الزمخشري وابن عطية
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya also parse “what she did of evil” as a relative subject whose predicate is “you wish”; they agree it cannot be a conditional clause because “you wish” is nominative, unless an omitted “she then wishes” is supplied, which is weak.
rows.anchor: بهذا الوجه بدأ الزمخشري وثنى به ابن عطية، واتفقا على أنه لا يجوز أن يكون: وما عملت من سوء، شرطا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan records that al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya rule out a conditional parse because “you wish” is nominative; Qadi al-Qudat al-Suruji challenged that view with a line by Zuhayr, prompting Abu Hayyan's grammatical inquiry.
rows.anchor: وظهر من كلاميهما امتناع الشرط لأجل رفع: تود، وهذه المسألة كان سألني عنها قاضي القضاة أبو العباس أحمد بن إبراهيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan sets out to show that when a conditional verb is past, a following present-tense verb that completes the condition-result construction may be either jussive or nominative.
rows.anchor: إذا كان فعل الشرط ماضيا، وما بعده مضارع تتم به جملة الشرط والجزاء، جاز في ذلك المضارع الجزم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous poet illustrates the nominative present after a past conditional with the example “if they ask for good, they give it.”
rows.anchor: إن يسألوا الخير يعطوه، وإن خبروا ... في الجهد أدرك منهم طيب أخبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan concludes that such nominative usage is frequent and supported by the grammarians, though they interpret it differently.
rows.anchor: فهذا الرفع، كما رأيت كثير، ونصوص الأمة على جوازه في الكلام

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر أحمد بن رشيد المالقي
rows.claim: Abu Ja'far al-Malaqi says he knows no such nominative usage and that analogy requires the jussive; he interprets reported examples by supplying an omitted fāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحبنا أبو جعفر أحمد بن رشيد المالقي، وهو مصنف (رصف المباني)

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh analyzes the nominative as fronted, with the actual conditional response omitted.
rows.anchor: فذهب سيبويه إلى أن ذلك على سبيل التقديم. وأما جواب الشرط فهو محذوف عنده

rows.speaker: الكوفيون وأبو العباس
rows.claim: The Kufis and Abu al-Abbas treat the nominative clause as the response itself, with its fāʾ omitted.
rows.anchor: وذهب الكوفيون، وأبو العباس إلى أنه هو الجواب حذفت منه الفاء

rows.speaker: غيرهما
rows.claim: Another analysis says that because the past conditional verb shows no effect of the conditional particle, the particle weakens before the present response, which is neither fronted nor prefixed by an omitted fāʾ; Abu Hayyan rejects this and the previous analysis as weak.
rows.anchor: وهذا والمذهب الذي قبله ضعيفان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan concludes that a nominative response does not prevent a conditional reading; “what she did” fails as the condition for a different reason, not because “you wish” is nominative.
rows.anchor: أن رفع المضارع لا يمنع أن يكون ما قبله شرطا، لكن امتنع أن يكون: وما عملت، شرطا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Sibawayh's fronting analysis, the pronoun in “between it” would refer to the conditional noun “what,” forcing a pronoun to precede its antecedent in an unlicensed construction.
rows.anchor: أن الضمير في قوله: وبينه، عائد على اسم الشرط الذي هو: ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan answers that a conditional clause would then require its evidence clause, although a condition governs only its result; this creates a contradiction absent in a single clause where verb, subject, and object share a governor.
rows.anchor: فتدافعا. وهذا بخلاف: ضرب زيدا غلامه، هي جملة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians allow “her slave struck Hind” because subject and object share a governor, but reject “her slave struck Hind's neighbor” because they do not; no Arabic usage supports the analogous problematic pronoun order.
rows.anchor: جاز عند بعضهم: ضرب غلامها هندا، لاشتراك الفاعل المضاف للضمير والمفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abdullah and Ibn Abi Abla read “what she did of evil, she wished,” permitting “what” to be a conditional noun in the accusative or, with al-Farra's omitted pronoun, nominative; “she wished” is then the result.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله، وابن أبي عبلة: من سوء ودت لو أن

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari prefers parsing the clause as a subject and predicate because it describes what happens on that Day and matches the majority reading.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: لكن الحمل على الابتداء والخبر أوقع في المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here law marks an unrealized consequence, with its response and the object of “you wish” omitted: the person wishes that the distance from the evil deed were long; the complement is a subject for Sibawayh and a subject-like agent for Abu al-Abbas.
rows.anchor: و: لو، هنا حرف لما كان سيقع لوقوع غيره، وجوابها محذوف، ومفعول: تود، محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Treating law as a source particle meaning “that” is remote because it would place one source particle directly before another, a rare pattern illustrated by 51:23; the meaning instead requires the law-clause to be the object of “you wish.”
rows.anchor: وأما على قول من يذهب إلى أن: لو، بمعنى: أن، وأنها مصدرية فهو بعيد هنا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the person wishes never to meet that deed again; this conveys the intended meaning.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: يسر أحدهم أن لا يلقى عمله ذلك أبدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative “whoever does that” points to their severing themselves from God's guardianship.
rows.anchor: والإشارة في قوله: ومن يفعل ذلك، الآية. أشار إلى انسلاخهم من ولاية الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan identifies a rhetorical emphasis in the phrases “what is in your breasts” and “what is in the heavens and earth.”
rows.anchor: والاختصاص في قوله: ما في صدوركم، وفي قوله: ما في السموات وما في الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reassurance that God is compassionate toward His servants comes after a passage that had caused apprehension.
rows.anchor: والتأنيس بعد الإيحاش في قوله: والله رؤوف بالعباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan notes ellipsis at several points in this passage, referring back to explanations already given in the commentary.
rows.anchor: والحذف في عدة مواضع تقدم ذكرها في التفسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is a firmly asserted divine statement settling the dispute; the majority take “this” to point to the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: هذا خبر من الله جزم مؤكد فصل به بين المختصمين، والإشارة إلى القرآن على قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن جريج وابن زيد وغيرهم
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd, and others take “this” to refer to the preceding account of Jesus, created without a father; it is the truth, against Jewish and Christian claims about him.
rows.anchor: قاله ابن عباس، وابن جريج، وابن زيد، وغيرهم. أي: هذا هو الحق لا ما يدعيه النصارى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view makes “this” point forward to “there is no god but God,” understanding the true report as God's oneness; Abu Hayyan says the syntax weighs against it because of the conjunction and emphatic construction.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هذا إشارة إلى ما بعده من قوله وما من إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr parses al-qaṣaṣ as the predicate of inna, with al-ḥaqq adjectival; al-qaṣaṣ can be a verbal noun or a passive noun meaning “what is recounted,” or huwa can be the subject with al-qaṣaṣ as predicate.
rows.anchor: والقصص خبر إن، والحق صفة له، والقصص مصدر، أو فعل بمعنى مفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the account true alludes to the fabricated story of Jesus' divinity advanced by Christians of Najran and others.
rows.anchor: ووصف القصص بالحق إشارة إلى القصص المكذوب الذي أتى به نصارى نجران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “There is no god but God” means only God possesses divinity and refutes dualists, Christians, and anyone who claims a deity besides Him.
rows.anchor: أي: المختص بالإلهية هو الله وحده، وفيه رد على الثنوية والنصارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min is extra for exhaustive generic negation; ilāh is a subject with an omitted predicate, while Allah is an appositive by syntactic position, not by surface case, since that would put the extra min in an affirmative clause.
rows.anchor: و: من، زائدة لاستغراق الجنس، و: إله، مبتدأ محذوف الخبر، و: الله، بدل منه على الموضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic permits an accusative after illā in this construction, but no reader uses it in this verse.
rows.anchor: ويجوز في العربية في نحو هذا التركيب نصب ما بعد: إلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two divine attributes signify irresistible power and knowledge expressed as wisdom and precision; neither attribute belongs to Jesus.
rows.anchor: وهاتان الصفتان منفيتان عن عيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parsing options for “He is surely” match those already discussed for “this is surely the true account.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز في: لهو، من الإعراب ما جاز في: لهو القصص

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the people turned away from the mutual imprecation.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: فإن تولوا عن الملاعنة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says they turned away from the clarification delivered by the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: عن البيان الذي أبانه رسول الله

rows.speaker: أبو سليمان الدمشقي
rows.claim: Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi says they turned away from affirming God's oneness and denying that He has a consort or child.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو سليمان الدمشقي: عن الإقرار بالوحدانية والتنزيه عن الصاحبة والولد

rows.speaker: المرسي
rows.claim: Al-Mursi says they turned away from this exhortation.
rows.anchor: وقال المرسي: عن هذا الذكر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes their turning away to mean turning away from faith.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عن الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether past tense or an imperfect with its second tāʾ omitted, the conditional's apparent response is “God knows the corrupters”; this names the resulting punishment by its cause and uses a general plural to include these people and others, also as a verse ending.
rows.anchor: وجواب الشرط في الظاهر الجملة من قوله: فإن الله عليم بالمفسدين

rows.speaker: الحسن والسدي ومحمد بن جعفر بن الزبير
rows.claim: Hasan, al-Suddi, and Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr say the verse was revealed concerning the delegation from Najran.
rows.anchor: نزلت في وفد نجران، قاله الحسن، والسدي، ومحمد بن جعفر بن الزبير

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says that after the people of Najran refused the invitation to mutual imprecation, they were invited to the easier common word.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد: لما أبى أهل نجران ما دعوا إليه من الملاعنة، دعوا إلى أيسر من ذلك
